entry.hook: Your next high-performing post is hiding in competitor comment sections.
entry.photocard_text: Search competitor comment sections for unanswered questions. Turn those exact friction points into your next tutorials.
entry.caption:
Whenever I plan a new content calendar for a client, I start by reading the comment sections of their five largest competitors.

Here is the exact framework you can run in twenty minutes:
First, locate high-performing posts from industry peers that generated dozens of comments.
Second, ignore the compliments and look specifically for user confusion, complaints, or unanswered questions. You will often see comments like "Does this integrate with Shopify?" or "How does this compare to standard retinol?"
Third, write dedicated posts answering those exact inquiries.

Your competitors spent money and time generating audience attention, but they rarely have the bandwidth to answer every nuanced question thoroughly. By stepping in and delivering direct answers through your own content, you attract buyers who are already evaluating solutions. It removes guesswork entirely from your content roadmap.

Founders frequently tell me they lack the creative inspiration to post regularly on LinkedIn. My answer is always the same: stop trying to be creative and start documenting what you already do.

Here is a simple system you can implement tomorrow:
Keep a blank digital document open during your daily operations. Whenever a client asks a clarifying question during an onboarding call, write it down word for word. Whenever a prospect explains why they chose you over a competitor, note the exact phrasing they used. At the end of the day, select one note and structure it into three short parts:
1. The specific problem encountered.
2. The solution you implemented.
3. The broader lesson for someone facing that issue.

Documenting customer interactions guarantees your content addresses actual buyer pain points. It transforms routine work into high-trust thought leadership.

I fixed this for myself and for clients by batching the thinking into one weekly sitting. I open the content pillars, pick one angle per pillar for the week, and write just the hook - one line, the idea that would make someone stop scrolling - for each planned post. That's it for the first pass. Only after all the hooks are down do I go back and write full captions, because writing five hooks back to back is a different, faster kind of thinking than writing five full posts one at a time with context-switching in between. The whole exercise takes under an hour once you've done it a few times, and it means you walk into the week already knowing what's going out and why, instead of improvising under a deadline. entry.hook: A simple way to tell if your hook actually works.
entry.photocard_text: Read only your first line out loud. If it doesn't make you want the next sentence, rewrite it before anything else.
entry.caption: Every post lives or dies in its first line, and most people write that line last, almost as an afterthought, after they've already written the body. I do the opposite now, and I tell every client to do the same: write the hook first, read it out loud by itself, and ask honestly whether it would make you stop scrolling if you saw it from a stranger's page. If the answer is no, don't touch the rest of the post yet - fix the hook first, because no amount of good content underneath a weak opening line will get read. A good hook usually does one of a few things: it names a specific, relatable problem, it makes a claim worth questioning, or it promises something concrete and useful in plain language. What it should never do is open with throat-clearing like "in today's digital age" or a generic greeting, because that's exactly where attention drops off fastest. Spend eighty percent of your editing time on the first line and the rest of the post gets dramatically easier to finish well.

entry.hook: A simple way to make your offers feel less pushy.
entry.photocard_text: Explain the problem the offer solves before mentioning the discount. People respond to the problem, not the percentage off.
entry.caption: Offers that lead straight with a discount percentage often get scrolled past, because the audience hasn't been reminded yet why they'd want the thing being discounted in the first place. A small change that consistently works better: open by naming the specific problem or moment the offer solves, then introduce the discount as the easy next step once that problem feels real to the reader. It reads less like a generic sale blast and more like a helpful nudge at the right moment. The offer itself doesn't need to change, just the order you present it in. If your promotions aren't converting the way you'd expect, this is one of the first things worth testing. Message us if you want a hand rewriting your next one.

entry.hook: The simplest fix for a page that feels inconsistent.
entry.photocard_text: Write down your 3 non-negotiables before your next post: tone, colors, and the one thing you never say. Check every post against them.
entry.caption: A lot of "our page doesn't feel like us" problems aren't creative problems, they're documentation problems - nobody ever wrote down what "us" actually means in concrete terms. The fastest fix I use with clients is a one-page brand check: three or four non-negotiables, written in plain language, that every single post has to pass before it goes out. That might be a tone rule ("friendly, never salesy"), a visual rule ("always use our two brand colors, never stock photo people"), and a content rule ("we never post without a clear takeaway for the reader"). It sounds almost too simple to matter, but having it written down turns a vague feeling of inconsistency into a two-minute checklist anyone on the team can run before hitting publish, including a social media manager who joined last month and never sat through the original branding conversation. If your page feels off but you can't say exactly why, that's usually the sign the rules only exist in someone's head instead of on paper.

entry.hook: The fastest way to get more comments on your posts.
entry.photocard_text: End with a specific, easy-to-answer question, not a generic "thoughts?". Specific questions get specific replies.
entry.caption: Ending a post with "thoughts?" rarely gets a response, because it's too open-ended for most people to bother answering. Swapping that for a specific, low-effort question - one with an easy, obvious answer like picking between two options or naming a favorite from a short list - tends to get noticeably more replies, because there's almost nothing to think about before typing one. More comments also tends to help the post get shown to more people in the first place, so this small wording change can have a bigger effect than it looks like it should. Try it on your next post and see what happens to your comment count. We're happy to help you brainstorm a few if you'd like.

entry.hook: A client once asked me to post more. I said no.
entry.photocard_text: More posts isn't always the right answer. Sometimes the honest advice is to slow down and fix the message first.
entry.caption: Early on I would have said yes to almost anything a client asked for, because saying no felt like risking the relationship. One client wanted to double posting frequency to "fix" flat engagement. I looked at the numbers first and the problem wasn't frequency, it was that the posts weren't saying anything a follower actually cared about - doubling a weak message just means twice as much of it gets ignored. I said so directly, laid out what I was seeing, and proposed we fix the message before touching the schedule. It was an uncomfortable conversation to start, but it was the right one, and it's a pattern I now watch for constantly: when a client asks for more volume, the real question is always whether the existing content earns more attention first. Agencies that just say yes to every request aren't being helpful, they're avoiding a harder conversation. The lesson I keep relearning is that giving honest, sometimes unwelcome advice early is what actually earns trust, not agreeing with everything a client suggests.

entry.hook: How to pick a cover photo that actually works for you.
entry.photocard_text: Your cover photo should answer "what do you do" in two seconds, not just look nice. Clarity beats decoration every time.
entry.caption: A cover photo is one of the first things a new visitor sees, and a purely decorative one - a nice scene with no information - wastes that first impression. The cover photos that work hardest answer "what does this business do" at a glance: a clear shot of the product, the storefront, or the service in action, sometimes with a short line of text if the image alone doesn't make it obvious. It doesn't need to be elaborate, just immediately clear. If someone unfamiliar with your business landed on your Page right now, would your cover photo tell them what you do within two seconds? If not, it's worth a quick update. We can help you put one together.
